title: Final Iteration and Risk Review (Lab)
summary: Students make their final improvement, sort risks on a likelihood-by-seriousness matrix, confirm the solution is safe and fair, and freeze the evaluated version for showcase.
objectives: Run a final evaluation across accuracy, usefulness and risk, and act on one improvement.
Complete a risk review and confirm the solution is safe and fair to use.
Document the final iteration with before-and-after evidence.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Time for the final polish. In this Lab you make your last improvement, then act like a safety checker, running a full risk review so you can promise your solution is safe and fair before showcase.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a final evaluation across accuracy, usefulness and risk and act on one improvement.
I can complete a risk review and confirm my solution is safe and fair.
I can record my final iteration with clear before-and-after evidence.

terms.definition: One more round of improving and re-testing.
How likely a risk is to actually happen.
How much harm a risk would cause if it happened.
A grid that sorts risks by likelihood and seriousness.
To stop changing the version you have evaluated.

sections.heading: Sorting risks the smart way
body: Not every risk is equal. A risk that is both likely and serious needs action now. A rare but very serious risk still needs a plan.
Place each risk on the [[risk matrix]], then decide: fix it now, or watch it. Always confirm no personal data is anywhere in your solution.

sections.heading: Finish, then freeze
body: Make your final planned change and re-test with known answers. Record before and after so others can trust your evidence.
Then **freeze** the version. The solution you show at the carousel must be the exact one you tested and judged safe.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: With your partner, make the final change, re-test, run the full risk review, and freeze your solution ready for showcase.
items: Set your Lab goal from the refinement log.
Re-test with at least five known-answer cases and record before and after.
List risks and place each on the matrix.
Decide actions and confirm no personal data is used.
Write a safe-and-fair statement and freeze the version.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which risk surprised you most when you placed it on the matrix?
How did freezing change how carefully you tested?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write your safe-and-fair statement in one sentence.
Name the risk you are most confident you have managed.

worksheet.title: Week 9 - Lab - Worksheet | Final Iteration and Risk Review (Lab)

questions.prompt: Match each position on the risk matrix to the decision the Lab says you should make.

left.text: A risk that is both likely to happen and serious
A risk that would rarely happen but would cause serious harm
A risk that is unlikely and would only be a small nuisance

right.text: Act on it now, before the showcase
Do not fix it now, but have a plan ready in case it happens
Leave it as it is and keep watching it

feedback.correct: Correct - the matrix decides the action: likely and serious means act now, rare but serious still needs a plan, and a small unlikely risk is only watched.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at how the Lab sorts risks: a risk that is both likely and serious needs action now, a rare but very serious risk still needs a plan, and a small unlikely one is just watched.

questions.prompt: In 1 test out of 20, Layla's classroom-finder sent a Grade 1 pupil to the wrong building. Her partner says: 'It only happened once, so it is not likely - leave it off the matrix.' Using the Lab's way of sorting risks, what should they do?

options.text: Place it as rare but serious, and write a plan for what to do if it does happen
Leave it off the matrix, because one wrong answer in twenty is not likely enough to count as a risk
Write it down as likely and serious, so that it definitely gets fixed before showcase
Judge it on likelihood alone, because the matrix is about how often a risk happens

feedback.correct: Correct - likelihood and seriousness are judged separately, so a rare risk that could really harm someone still goes on the matrix with a plan.
feedback.incorrect: Rare does not mean safe. The matrix uses two axes, so a risk that is unlikely but would seriously harm a young pupil still belongs on it, with a plan.

questions.prompt: A team freezes their version, then on the morning of the carousel they spot one more small improvement, add it without re-testing, and tell the audience what they changed. Does this follow the Lab's rule about freezing?

feedback.correct: Correct - freezing means the version you show is the exact one you tested and judged safe, so announcing a late change does not make it allowed.
feedback.incorrect: Telling the audience does not fix it: an untested change means the solution on show is no longer the one the evidence and the safe-and-fair statement cover.

questions.prompt: Before a team can freeze their solution for the showcase, which of these must they be able to show? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Before-and-after results from re-testing with known-answer cases
A check confirming that no personal data is used anywhere in the solution
Each risk placed on the matrix by likelihood and seriousness, with the action they decided
A new feature added after the final round of testing
Proof that there are no risks left on their matrix at all

feedback.correct: Correct - a frozen solution comes with before-and-after evidence, a completed matrix with actions, and a privacy check.
feedback.incorrect: Freezing needs three things in place: before-and-after results from re-testing, every risk placed on the matrix with an action decided, and a confirmation that no personal data is used.

questions.prompt: Complete this team's final Lab statement: 'We sorted every risk by how likely it is and how ___ the harm would be. We checked that no ___ data is used anywhere in our solution. Then we ___ the version, so the one we show at the carousel is exactly the one we tested.'
blanks: the kind of data that must not be there
what you do to the tested version

feedback.correct: Correct - the matrix uses likelihood and seriousness together, the privacy check removes personal data, and freezing keeps the tested version the one on show.
feedback.incorrect: The matrix's second axis is how serious the harm would be; the privacy check is about personal data; and stopping all further changes to the tested version is called freezing it.

formative.targets: Self- and peer-evaluation against the tiered rubric (Emerging = expected)
formative.check: Final iteration completed and a full risk review with a safe-and-fair statement
formative.successCriteria: Meets the Emerging criteria; completes a risk matrix, acts on one improvement, and confirms no personal data is used.
formative.evidence: Final iteration log + completed risk matrix + safe-and-fair statement.
